name: WiFi Deauther
firmware: Deauther V2 (Maltronics fork of SpacehuhnTech esp8266_deauther)
firmware_note: Maltronics' own public fork of Stefan Kremser's (Spacehuhn) open-source ESP8266 Deauther v2 firmware, pre-flashed onto a sealed ESP8266 board. The README does not document any functional changes from upstream beyond branding; the same firmware compiles for free onto any ~$3-6 NodeMCU or Wemos D1 Mini.
price_note: Listed at GBP 37.00 on the vendor site; converted at the GBP/USD rate on 2026-09-10 (~1.356). Price buys a case, an RGB LED, and dual USB-A/USB-C wiring on top of a bare ESP8266 module.
skill_note: Pre-flashed, controlled entirely through a phone or laptop browser hitting the device's own web UI; no coding needed for stock use.
build_note: Ready to use out of the box. The case is sealed with no accessible GPIO, so there is nothing to extend or reflash without opening it.
summary: A sealed, pre-flashed ESP8266 board in a small metallic USB-stick case running Maltronics' fork of the open-source Spacehuhn ESP8266 Deauther v2 firmware. It scans nearby Wi-Fi networks and clients, then sends 802.11 deauthentication frames to disconnect them, plus beacon-frame and probe-request spam, all driven from a phone or laptop browser hitting its built-in web UI.
honest_take: This is a $3-6 ESP8266 dev board running firmware that Spacehuhn/SpacehuhnTech gives away free on GitHub; Maltronics' fork adds nothing beyond the case, an RGB LED, and USB-A/USB-C wiring, so most of the ~$45 premium over a bare board buys convenience and cosmetics, not capability. It is not a jammer - it sends spoofed management frames, and those only work against networks that don't enforce 802.11w/PMF, which WPA3 makes mandatory, so it increasingly does nothing against modern APs. The case is sealed with no exposed GPIO, so unlike a bare dev board you can't repurpose it for anything else once you're done deauthing.
best_for: Learning how 802.11 management-frame deauth attacks work
Quick demonstrations of weaknesses in open (non-PMF) Wi-Fi networks
not_for: Attacking WPA3 or any 802.11w/PMF-protected network
Actual RF jamming - it sends frames, not noise
Anything beyond 2.4GHz Wi-Fi - no sub-GHz, NFC, or BLE hardware

The exact module package (ESP-12F, ESP-07S, etc.) inside the current sealed case is not published; earlier, now-discontinued Maltronics deauther SKUs used ESP-12 (4MB flash) and ESP-07 (1MB flash) variants.

summary: A tiny 802.11n travel router built around a Qualcomm Atheros AR9331 SoC, sold here at a markup specifically because the reflashing community (OpenWrt, MiniPwner) validated years ago that this model works as a pocket-sized pentest dropbox. The unit itself ships with stock TP-Link firmware - it is not preloaded with OpenWrt or MiniPwner.
honest_take: This SKU is bare, unmodified TP-Link firmware - Hacker Warehouse is charging $50 for a router that sells for $15-25 elsewhere, and the entire premium is 'we know this specific model works for MiniPwner,' not anything they've done to the hardware. Worse, OpenWrt itself now actively discourages this device: its 4MB flash/32MB RAM is officially flagged as too small for any OpenWrt release newer than 19.07 (last built 2022), so a buyer chasing a modern, patched OpenWrt dropbox will not get one on this hardware - you're building on a permanently frozen, unpatched base. MiniPwner itself is a real, well-documented project dating to 2012 (Kevin Bong and Michael Vieau), not a marketing name, but its guides and package set (Aircrack-ng, Kismet, Nmap, Reaver, etc.) predate modern Wi-Fi security and haven't seen meaningful updates in years.

On Core2 it covers scanning, deauth, captive-portal credential capture, karma attacks, beacon spam, handshake capture, a basic LAN toolkit (rogue DHCP/DNS, port scanning), and Flipper/skimmer/deauth detection; the fuller module set (BadUSB, IMSI catcher, LLM chat, IR) is Cardputer-only.
honest_take: This is firmware for the plain ESP32 inside a Core2, not a purpose-built security device - the same Xtensa LX6 silicon is in $5 dev boards, and the $42.90 buys you the screen, battery, case and Grove ports, not any special radio capability. The project's own README recommends the Cardputer over the Core2 ('Better one: M5Cardputer'), and its own feature matrix confirms it: Core2 gets deauth, karma, captive portals and a basic LAN toolkit, but not BadUSB, IMSI catching, IR or the 'Wardriving Master' multi-node mode. Deauth and beacon spam only reach unprotected management frames - WPA3's mandatory PMF stops it like every other ESP32 tool. And the credential-harvesting captive portal plus rogue-DHCP/DNS features push this well past 'harmless Wi-Fi scanner' territory some buyers expect - using them against a network you don't own is a computer-misuse-shaped decision, not a grey area.

summary: ESP32 Wardriver Pro is a solo-maintained, deliberately minimal wardriving logger: an ESP32 DevKit board, a GPS module, a small OLED and a microSD card, wired together and flashed with an Arduino sketch that scans Wi-Fi, waits for a GPS fix, and writes properly-formatted WigleWifi-1.4 CSV rows to the SD card. honest_take: The 'passive' framing is honest about intent but worth reading precisely: the underlying WiFi.scanNetworks() call is Arduino's standard active station-mode scan, which transmits 802.11 probe requests on every channel to elicit responses - the same thing your phone does constantly, not a promiscuous-mode radio that only listens. What 'passive' actually means here is narrower and true: no deauth, no packet injection, no joining networks, confirmed directly in the source (WifiScanner.cpp calls nothing but WiFi.scanNetworks). The upside of that narrow scope is real: this is a solo hobby project (40 stars) that still shipped exactly what it says it does - a genuine WigleWifi-1.4 CSV with a correct header - unlike wardriver3000 (also in this database), whose custom PCB and README both promise Wigle compatibility that its own firmware doesn't deliver. Against JCMK's actively-maintained 'C5 Wardriver' (dual-band 2.4+5GHz, BLE, also correctly WiGLE-formatted, from the same team behind ESP32 Marauder), this is the honest budget pick if you specifically want 2.4GHz-only passive logging and don't mind wiring your own board from loose modules - the C5 Wardriver adds 5GHz and BLE for not much more cost and effort, and has a larger, more active community behind it.

name: WiFi Dev Board GPS Expansion
firmware_note: This is a passive adapter board with no firmware of its own - it exposes GPS and microSD to whichever firmware the host Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board (an ESP32-S2 board made by Flipper Devices, not JCMK) is running. In practice that means ESP32 Marauder, the only Dev Board firmware with code paths that use SD storage and GPS for wardriving/pcap logging.
price_note: Sold out at the vendor as of this check, no restock date given.
skill_note: The vendor describes soldering the adapter PCB directly against the back of the Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board, joint by joint ('no wires needed') - fine hand-soldering on an already-populated board, not a beginner's first solder job.
build_note: Solder-on adapter, confirmed by the vendor's own product description: 'placing the adapter PCB against the back of the Flipper Zero WiFi Dev Board and soldering each connection.' Ships with the adapter PCB and a ceramic GPS antenna; no wiring harness.
summary: A small adapter PCB from JCMK (the ESP32 Marauder developer's company) that solders onto the back of the official Flipper Zero Wi-Fi Dev Board (an ESP32-S2 board made by Flipper Devices, which has no SD slot or GPS of its own) to add a microSD slot, a GPS receiver with ceramic antenna, and UART activity LEDs. It exists specifically to give that board's ESP32 Marauder firmware somewhere to write pcap captures and Wigle-format wardrive logs, and a GPS fix to tag them with.
honest_take: This only makes sense if you already own three separate things: a Flipper Zero, the official ESP32-S2 Wi-Fi Dev Board (sold separately by Flipper Devices), and now this $21 adapter - plus a soldering iron. The Wi-Fi Dev Board's ESP32-S2 has no Bluetooth at all (S2 silicon lacks it) and 2.4GHz-only Wi-Fi, so this expansion doesn't add any radio capability - it only adds the storage and positioning that Marauder's wardriving and pcap-capture modes need. The 'UART activity LEDs' are exactly what they sound like: two indicator LEDs so you can tell serial traffic is flowing without hooking up a logic analyzer, not a new interface. If GPS wardriving is the actual goal rather than stacking accessories onto a Flipper you already own, JCMK's own 'C5 Wardriver' or Marauder v8 board (both already in this database) get you dual-band Wi-Fi, GPS and SD in one purchase with no soldering.
